source: Veale, O'Donoghue, Keane (2000) Computation and Blending
finding: Fauconnier and Turner's network adds a generic space and a blend space to the classic two-space (source/target) model of metaphor. Generic space holds the low-level shared structure that lets the inputs be aligned. The blend is a new space that can grow emergent structure on its own.
numbers: Four spaces: two inputs, generic, blend. Example: Scientist and Priest aligned as lab=church, lab-bench=altar, method=dogma. Black Hole blend: Blackness input conflicts with Hole input, so the blend has traits neither input has.
quote: generic space that captures the common background knowledge that unites the inputs
limits: A secondary description by computational modellers, not the founding paper.
agent_relevance: Our schema could name the shared abstraction (generic space) explicitly before any merge of two ideas.

source: Veale, O'Donoghue, Keane (2000) Computation and Blending
finding: Five optimality constraints define a well-formed blend: integration, web, unpacking, topology, good reason. They are not orthogonal, so no blend meets all of them perfectly.
numbers: 5 constraints in this account. Topology example: Church relates to Altar as Laboratory relates to Lab-Bench.
limits: Other writings by the theory's authors give different lists. The constraints were never turned into a single measurable test.
agent_relevance: The constraints work as a checklist for judging a model-made blend: can a reader unpack it, and do relations keep their shape.

source: Veale, O'Donoghue, Keane (2000) Computation and Blending
finding: Sapper, a spreading-activation graph matcher, is argued to be the model closest to blending. It builds bridges with two rules: triangulation (two concepts share a neighbour) and squaring (an existing bridge links neighbours). Active bridges stand for the blend space; dormant bridges stand for the network. A fifth 'constructor space' of mapping rules is proposed.
numbers: Compared with SME, ACME, Tabletop, LISA. Surgeon-General example: Enemy-Soldier maps to Cancer-Cell, or Enemy-Army to Bacteria, but not both. Example activation threshold 0.01; 10% attenuation per arc.
quote: a maximal collection of mutually systematic bridges, each bridge representing a fusion of counterpart elements
limits: Argued from examples. No benchmark and no human data.
agent_relevance: A blend should keep a maximal set of mutually consistent correspondences. A program can check that consistency; the model need not.

source: Veale (2002) How to Blend Concepts and Influence People
finding: Journal version of the same computational account. It repeats that blending theory must be shown tractable and constrained to avoid 'just-so' stories.
numbers: Text of the theory section matches the 2000 chapter.
limits: Near-duplicate of a02-a03. Not an independent confirmation.
agent_relevance: Count as one source, not two.

source: Turner (2014) Challenges to Blending Theory
finding: Turner concedes the evidence is mostly indirect: generalisations fitted to in-sample data (for example grammar patterns), then checked on out-of-sample data. He says brain imaging is too gross to isolate blending, and that the process 'does not appear to me to be algorithmic'.
numbers: Cites McCubbins and Turner (2013) experiments on easier and harder blend patterns. No effect sizes on the page.
quote: does not appear to me to be algorithmic
limits: Author's own defence. The replies are argument, not data.
agent_relevance: The theory is a framework, not a tested mechanism. Use blending as a prompt-structure heuristic, not as a validated law.

source: Wikipedia (accessed 2026) Conceptual blending
finding: Canonical vocabulary. Emergent structure comes by composition, completion and elaboration (running the blend). Four network types: simplex, mirror, single-scope, double-scope. Vital relations include time, cause-effect, change, space, identity, role, part-whole. Koestler's monk riddle is a mirror network.
numbers: Monk riddle: put both journeys on one day and two monks must meet. Development began 1993; Fauconnier and Turner 1998 Cognitive Science 22(2):133-187.
limits: Encyclopedia summary, used only to fix terms.
agent_relevance: Composition-completion-elaboration maps to three steps: merge, add background knowledge, simulate the result.

source: Gibbs (2000) Making good psychology out of blending theory; Ritchie (2004) Lost in conceptual space (second-hand)
finding: Critiques as reported by secondary pages: blending lacks testable hypotheses, works as a framework, infers processes from products, and other theories explain the same data. Ritchie says many blends fit simpler processes. Others say the theory is unfalsifiable and 'anything goes'; the optimality principles were the reply.
numbers: No numbers. Gibbs is Cognitive Linguistics 11(3/4).
limits: Originals not opened. Only summaries seen.
agent_relevance: Overgeneration is the known weakness: any two things can be merged. The agent needs a filter step.

source: Coulson and Van Petten (2002) Conceptual integration and metaphor: an event-related potential study
finding: A rare direct human test tied to blending. Adults read sentences ending literally, metaphorically, or in an intermediate 'literal mapping' condition. N400 at 300-500 ms was smallest for literal, largest for metaphorical, intermediate for literal mapping. Metaphorical endings also gave a larger late posterior positivity. Authors say it fits blending: integration demands change difficulty for literal and metaphorical language alike.
numbers: N = 18 adults. Effect sizes not obtained.
limits: Only a paraphrased abstract was seen. A later commentary says cloze probability was controlled but novelty and complexity were not, so other explanations remain.
agent_relevance: More cross-domain mapping costs more effort, so blend prompts may need clearer scaffolding.

source: Eppe, Maclean, Confalonieri, Kutz, Schorlemmer, Plaza, Kuhnberger (2018) A computational framework for conceptual blending
finding: COINVENT framework. Generalising the input concepts is a search problem solved with answer set programming. Metrics approximate the optimality principles and prune blends. Applied to invent concepts in mathematics and music.
numbers: EU grant FET-Open 611553. Artificial Intelligence 256:105-129. No benchmark numbers retrieved.
limits: Full text could not be fetched (connection refused). Facts come from a search summary only.
agent_relevance: A formal route: generalise inputs to a shared theory, combine, rank with metrics. That is search plus pruning, not free generation.

source: Diaconescu (2017) 3/2-institutions: an institution theory for conceptual blending
finding: Mathematical formalisation. Goguen axiomatised blending in category theory (blends as colimits, later lax cocones with model amalgamation). This paper extends institution theory to partial signature morphisms, driven by blending. The COINVENT project followed Goguen's line.
numbers: Theory paper. No experiments.
limits: Abstract maths with no test against human blends.
agent_relevance: The core operation is a structured combination of theories with consistency checks. That is code-checkable.

source: Ge and Parikh (2021) Visual Conceptual Blending with Large-scale Language and Vision Models
finding: A language model proposes a related object and a one-sentence blend description. CLIP-guided BigSleep and DeepDaze draw it. On a simile dataset, language models beat ConceptNet at proposing the right property, and larger models did better. Mechanical Turk raters preferred the large-model images over a GAN baseline.
numbers: P@1000 on the simile task: best language model 66.38, BERT-base 5.90 (row labels in the extracted table are unclear). 20 blend descriptions, 6 questions per image pair, 3 model pairs. 96.34% of objects found in ConceptNet; 688.9 relations returned on average when 1000 requested.
limits: Early (2021) models. Small human study. Table labels garbled in the text extract.
agent_relevance: Proposing the connecting property is a step LLMs do well, better than a knowledge base.

source: Wang, Petridis, Kwon, Ma, Chilton (2023) PopBlends: Strategies for Conceptual Blending with Large Language Models
finding: GPT-3 plus retrieval suggests connecting concepts between a pop-culture domain and a product. In a within-subject study of 10 students the tool gave more blend ideas and lower workload than web search.
numbers: Ideas per pair 2.03 (SD 0.84) vs 0.87 (SD 0.56), Wilcoxon p<0.001. All 10 preferred it. NASA-TLX mental demand 2.85 vs 5.80 (p=0.004); effort 3.05 vs 5.00 (p=0.006); frustration 1.65 vs 3.25 (p=0.026). GPT-3 attribute accuracy 57% overall: adjectives 79%, activities 58%, catchphrases 35%. Connecting-concept accuracy 56.0, 55.3, 58.7% for three strategies; at least one of five correct for 93.3% of pairs.
limits: N = 10 amateur designers, one baseline (web search), Bonferroni over 6 tests. About half of suggestions are wrong.
agent_relevance: Ask for five candidates and pick one: about 93% coverage despite about 57% per-item accuracy. Fits generate-many-then-select.

source: Peng, Ma, Wang, Wang, Wang, Zhang, Zhu, Zheng (2025) Probing and Inducing Combinational Creativity in Vision-Language Models
finding: Builds a three-level Identification-Explanation-Implication (IEI) framework from blending theory and 666 artist-made visual mashups. Best vision-language models beat average people at understanding blends, but not experts. Adding the explanation step to image-generation prompts raised ranked quality, and not because prompts were longer.
numbers: Implication win rate: experts 78.3, GPT-4o 73.5, GPT-4V 71.9, Gemini-1.5-Pro 71.7, Claude-3.5-Sonnet 62.9, average people 51.0, Claude-3-Opus 39.2, LLaVA-1.5-7B 20.1. Identification precision/recall: GPT-4o 75.67/85.00, people 53.42/70.33. GPT-4o judge agreed with two experts 85.1% and 81.6% on 200 pairs. Prompt length IEI 514.53 vs II 487.95 (p=0.404). Midjourney win rate 0.26 to 0.35 with IEI. Mean rank IEI 1.98, II 2.40.
limits: Model (GPT-4o) is the judge for most scores. Human sample size not stated in the part read. Image task.
agent_relevance: Naming the inputs, then shared attributes, then the implication improved output without extra length. A cheap three-slot scaffold.

source: Peng et al. (2025) IEI: fusion versus replacement and the render gap
finding: Fusion mashups (traits of both objects kept) were easier to decompose than replacement mashups, in 9 of 11 models. The text-to-image step, not the idea step, was the bottleneck.
numbers: 90% (36/40) DALLE-3 examples integrated the objects; 27.8% (10/36) of well-written descriptions failed to render well.
limits: Small sample (40 items) for the 90% figure. The 'fusion easier' direction is inconsistent in the paper text (one caption says replacement is higher).
agent_relevance: Idea quality and execution quality fail separately; check them separately.

source: Schapiro et al. (2026) Measuring Combinatorial Creativity in Large Language Models and Humans (KOMBINE)
finding: Open-ended benchmark of association, analogy and blending between random entity pairs: 35 LLMs, 75 humans. Blending is hardest for both. LLMs hit an abstraction bottleneck: they rarely find a valid generic space, but once they do, they almost always write a coherent blend.
numbers: Valid blends: LLMs 43.4% vs humans 12.8%. Analogies 53.4% vs 32.9%. Associations 59.0% vs 22.1%. LLMs 10-16 points worse on blends than on the other two. Generic space found 43.4% of the time; coherent blend given a valid generic space 97.1%. Blend scores: gpt-5.6-sol 64.8, gemini-3.1-pro 59.5, gpt-6-astra 56.5, claude-fable-5 45.7, claude-opus-4.6 41.4, grok-4.6 35.0.
limits: Judged by three LLMs. Reliability ICC(2,3): blend integration quality 0.67, blend utility 0.48. Human vs panel majority agreement 66% over 150 judgements; 75% when the panel was unanimous (n=96). Scores are percent of max of a composite. Version read was v6.
agent_relevance: Names where blending fails: the shared abstraction. A step that forces the model to state and test the generic space first targets that bottleneck.

source: Schapiro et al. (2026) Measuring Combinatorial Creativity in Large Language Models and Humans (KOMBINE): inventive homogeneity
finding: Different LLMs invent the same blends. Of 2,070 invented concepts with 7,868 properties, 19.9% (412) reused two or more near-identical properties from another model's concept for the same item.
numbers: Blends vs analogies at level 2: 37.3% vs 2.6% (14.3x); level 1: 94.7% vs 36.3% (2.6x). Same provider 9.3% vs different provider 4.1% (2.3x). Anthropic +11.1 and DeepSeek +12.2 points over baseline; OpenAI -1.4. Threshold 0.674 cosine (99th percentile).
limits: Embedding-based sameness test, so it measures meaning overlap, not strict identity.
agent_relevance: Many blends from one model family are correlated. Mix providers or force distinct generic spaces.

source: Schapiro et al. (2026) Measuring Combinatorial Creativity in Large Language Models and Humans (KOMBINE): association as predictor
finding: Across models, association originality best predicts the other facets, in line with Mednick. Correlations: original analogies r=0.73, surprising analogies r=0.63, original blends r=0.42, surprising blends r=0.50, valid blends r=0.48.
numbers: p: <1e-4, 6e-5, 1e-2, 2e-3, 3e-3. Mean cross-task r 0.47. n = 35 models.
limits: Correlations are over 35 models, not items. Judges are LLMs.
agent_relevance: Models good at far association also blend better, so far-association tests are a cheap proxy for the blend step.

source: Schapiro et al. (2026) Measuring Combinatorial Creativity in Large Language Models and Humans (KOMBINE): analogy versus blending
finding: Authors argue analogy and blending are not exclusive: the main product of a blend is a blended space with emergent structure. They note blending overlaps least with compositional generalisation, since it needs abstraction and emergent elaboration. Their rule: a genuine blend has at least one 'uv' triple (a property both inputs feed) and at least one 'emergent' triple (true of the blend, of neither input).
numbers: Judge panel scores generic-space utility, coherence and emergent integration.
limits: Operational definition chosen by the benchmark authors.
agent_relevance: A code-checkable test of a blend: one shared slot plus one emergent property.

source: Schapiro et al. (2026) Measuring Combinatorial Creativity in Large Language Models and Humans (KOMBINE): human versus LLM semantic regions
finding: Humans and LLMs use different regions of semantic space. On association LLMs name more people (+5.2 points) and places (+3.6); humans use more physical objects (+3.0) and states (+2.4).
numbers: Frequency gaps in percentage points over WordNet noun and verb categories.
limits: Category labels are coarse.
agent_relevance: Mixing human and model input widens coverage of ideas.

source: Xu, Zhang, Gao, Deussen, Lee, Tang (2026) Beyond Pixels: Visual Metaphor Transfer via Schema-Driven Agentic Reasoning
finding: Multi-agent system encoding blending as a 'Schema Grammar' (subject, carrier, relational invariant, violation, emergent meaning), with Perception, Transfer, Generation and Diagnosis agents and backtracking. A strong one-shot prompt that contains the same theory description does worse than the staged system.
numbers: Human study N = 100 (age 14-55), 5-point scales. Ablation table, ingenuity: direct prompt 2.75, strong prompt 3.69, no CBT text 3.66, no transfer agent 3.71, no diagnosis 4.05, full 4.56 (main text says 4.61). Appropriateness: 2.96, 3.77, 3.68, 3.83, 3.98, 4.51. Pairwise preference for full system: 64.44% vs GPT-Image, 67.11% vs Banana-pro, 72.89% vs Midjourney, 76.22% vs BAGEL; worse in under 10% of pairs.
limits: Image domain. Table and text numbers differ slightly. Part of the scoring used Gemini, GPT and Claude as judges.
agent_relevance: Theory text alone in a prompt is not enough. Staged steps plus a diagnose-and-revise loop added gain, matching our design where the program drives stages.

source: Matsuhira, Kastner, Komamizu, Hirayama, Ide (2024) Investigating Conceptual Blending of a Diffusion Model for Improving Nonword-to-Image Generation
finding: Stable Diffusion shows blending when fed the midpoint of two CLIP text embeddings. Measured on 1,000 nouns.
numbers: Midpoint: blended-concept depiction ratio 0.621, mixed-concept ratio 0.862. Averaged over all interpolation ratios: 0.389 and 0.471. Proposed estimator FID to ground truth 1.86 at k=300.
limits: Image diffusion only. Interpolation is not selective projection.
agent_relevance: Latent midpoints mix indiscriminately; text blends need selective projection, which a scaffold has to supply.

source: Sato (2025) The Way We Prompt: Conceptual Blending, Neural Dynamics, and Prompt-Induced Transitions in LLMs
finding: Essay using blending as a lens on prompts. Defines Prompt-Induced Transition (shift of tone or meaning) and Prompt-Induced Hallucination (plausible but ungrounded text from fusing distant domains, for example the periodic table plus tarot).
numbers: No numbers or controlled experiment in the part read.
limits: Anecdotal and conceptual. A hypothesis source only.
agent_relevance: Fusing distant domains can give confident nonsense, so a blend output needs a grounding check.

source: Song et al. (2025) and Wang et al. (2023), as cited in KOMBINE
finding: As cited: LLMs of 2025 struggle to write noun-phrase combinations with emergent properties (the 'white' in 'peeled apple').
numbers: No numbers in the citing text.
limits: Second-hand. The Song paper was not opened.
agent_relevance: Emergence is weak even for easy two-word combinations.

source: Hampton (1987) and Wilkenfeld and Ward (2001) on emergent features in conceptual combination (not retrieved)
finding: Attempted to retrieve the classic human work on emergent attributes in combined concepts. The PubMed search returned no result and no full text was found, so no figures are recorded.
numbers: None.
limits: Gap: no human emergence rates or alignable-difference effects obtained.
agent_relevance: Treat emergence effects as unquantified in this file.

source: Veale, O'Donoghue, Keane (2000) Computation and Blending: slippage
finding: Strict isomorphism is too rigid for many blends. A Tabletop-style slipnet softens Sapper's rules so non-isomorphic structures can map, for example a Scalpel treated as a type of Cleaver. The authors say some contexts need isomorphism dropped altogether.
numbers: Core slippage rule uses a probability of slipping between relations above a minimal rigidity threshold. No evaluation numbers.
limits: Design sketch only; not tested against human judgements.
agent_relevance: A blend step needs a tunable strictness: strict mapping for checking, loose mapping for generating.
